evaluation.positioning_hook: A timid office clerk with erased memories is forced into a monster-hunting squad, only to discover his uselessness may be the most dangerous power in the room.

audience_appeal_marketability.reasoning: The premise is immediately legible and built for genre audiences: a reluctant desk worker gets dragged into a violent supernatural team-up, with a clear underdog hook. The appeal is narrower than a four-quadrant crowd-pleaser because the humor is very specific and the world is stylized, but the action-comedy engine is easy to sell.

conceptual_hook_clarity.reasoning: The hook lands fast in the opening pages: Francis is a logistics worker at Comirum, gets conscripted, and is revealed to be a SINON whose power is anomalous and potentially anything. The mission structure and the wrist-meter create a clean, explainable engine.

character_appeal_and_long_term_potential.reasoning: Francis has a strong built-in contradiction — anxious pencil pusher versus latent godlike weapon — and the team around him is colorful enough to support scenes. The supporting players are vivid, but the script is still mostly powered by Francis's confusion rather than deep interpersonal turns.

creative_originality_and_boldness.reasoning: The script has a confident, weirdly specific voice: retro-futuristic bureaucracy, comic-sans death toll boards, multilingual banter, and a British zombie target all give it a distinct identity. It feels like a writer making deliberate tonal choices rather than following a template.

narrative_momentum_engagement.reasoning: Once Doreen recruits Francis, the script moves with real urgency toward the London fight, and the wrist percentage gives the action a ticking-clock feel. The middle is more setup-heavy than the premise promises, but the final stretch escalates cleanly into payoff.

resonant_originality.reasoning: The core idea is fresh in a way that clicks quickly: a powerless office drone may secretly be the most dangerous person in a monster-killing unit. It is not yet in the rarefied territory of a truly iconic premise, but it has a memorable, ownable contradiction.

world_density_and_texture.reasoning: Comirum feels like a functioning institution with its own hierarchy, slang, and absurd internal logic, from the death-toll board to the SINON classification system. The team roster and mission rules suggest a larger ecosystem beyond this one assignment.

tonal_specificity.reasoning: The tone is unusually specific: deadpan workplace comedy colliding with grotesque supernatural action and cartoonish profanity. The script knows exactly how silly it wants to be without losing the threat of the monster fight.

latent_depth_slow_burn_potential.reasoning: Francis's opening flash of the empty college ruins and the erased-glasses image suggest a deeper mystery around his memory and power. That said, the page is still mostly operating as a launchpad, so the deeper emotional or mythic layer is implied more than dramatized.

relationship_density_and_ensemble_engine.reasoning: The team dynamic is already doing work: Francis and Ploy have chemistry, Hal and Clara have a lived-in banter rhythm, and Toast/Doreen add friction. Multiple pairings can generate scenes, which is a strong sign for repeatable ensemble energy.

lead_characters.name: Francis Booker
lead_characters.demographics: Male, early 20s to early 30s, office worker, anomalous superpowered human
lead_characters.hook: A nervous logistics clerk at Comirum who would rather hide behind spreadsheets than go into the field, Francis is the kind of reluctant lead who becomes interesting because he is so visibly outmatched. He starts as a dead-end bureaucrat with a mysterious power meter on his wrist and ends the script as the one person who can erase a monster, even if he still barely understands how.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the showcase territory of Jesse Eisenberg in The Social Network or Simon Pegg in Shaun of the Dead — fast, brittle, self-protective comedy that can flip into genuine heroism. The role gives an actor the chance to play panic, timing, and a late-blooming power reveal in the same frame.

lead_characters.name: Doreen
lead_characters.hook: Doreen is the hard-edged boss who knows exactly how broken the system is and still keeps it moving. She has the authority of a field commander and the weariness of someone who has already made peace with ugly compromises.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that gives an actor the clipped command energy of Jodie Foster in Contact or Carrie-Anne Moss in Jessica Jones — controlled, unsentimental, and quietly intimidating. The showcase is authority under pressure, with just enough humanity leaking through to make the character memorable.

lead_characters.name: Ploy
lead_characters.hook: Ploy is the loud, flirtatious, bass-loving operative who treats danger like a social event and seems to enjoy chaos more than safety. Under the swagger, she is also the first person to clock Francis's potential and push him toward it.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of part that gives an actor the fizzy, scene-stealing freedom of Awkwafina in The Farewell or Tessa Thompson in Thor: Ragnarok — comic velocity with real emotional intelligence underneath. The role lets someone dominate a room, then pivot into genuine ally energy.

lead_characters.name: Hal
lead_characters.hook: Hal is the swaggering frontline fighter who talks like a legend and gets treated like a joke by everyone around him, which only makes him more committed to the bit. He is all bravado, appetite, and bruiser confidence, but the script keeps him likable enough to anchor the team’s physical energy.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the showcase lane of Dave Bautista in Guardians of the Galaxy or John Cena in Peacemaker — a big physical presence who can sell both comedy and threat. The role gives an actor room to play size, timing, and wounded pride without becoming a straight parody.

lead_characters.name: Clara
lead_characters.hook: Clara is the coked-up, knife-catching, gun-toting chaos agent who seems permanently one bad decision away from disaster and one good line away from stealing the scene. She is flirtatious, reckless, and weirdly competent, which makes her one of the script’s sharpest comic weapons.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of part that gives an actor the feral comic snap of Jennifer Coolidge in The White Lotus or Kathryn Hahn in WandaVision — outrageous behavior with precision underneath. The showcase is volatility that still reads as control.

lead_characters.name: Toast
lead_characters.hook: Toast is the dry, superior robot teammate who treats everyone else like an inferior species while still functioning as part of the squad. The character’s appeal is in the contrast between his cold logic and the messy, chaotic humans around him.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that lets an actor do deadpan precision in the vein of Alan Tudyk’s robot work or Ben Schwartz’s voice-driven comedy — all timing, no vanity. The showcase is comic disdain with a mechanical edge.

lead_characters.name: Jerry
lead_characters.hook: Jerry is the friendly, hungry, physically oddball coworker who makes the world feel lived-in by being both monstrous and mundane. He is a small but effective texture character, the kind of presence that tells you this office has a whole ecosystem of weirdos.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is a fun character-actor slot in the mold of Doug Jones creature work or a Ron Perlman-style genre supporting turn — memorable physicality with a single comic beat. The role is about making a strange world feel normal.

casting_characteristics: ensemble of highly stylized supporting roles

locations.interior_exterior_ratio: mostly interiors with one major exterior action sequence
notable_requirements: office floor with cubicles and briefing room

technical.vfx_details: multicolor energy effects, wrist-device UI, teleportation flashes, monster regeneration/glitch effects, and a beam-based power climax
technical.sfx_needs: prosthetic zombie/monster makeup, practical blood, limb-loss gags, weapon transformation effects, and breakaway glass

platform_fit.series_engine_or_release_model: Feature release model; best suited to streamer-first or genre-friendly theatrical distribution

budget.note: The office material is contained, but the London night fight adds VFX, prosthetics, weapon effects, and rooftop/street coverage that will keep this above a simple contained indie.

casting.note: Francis needs a very specific comic-anxious lead who can pivot into power without losing likability, and the ensemble depends on sharply differentiated supporting players rather than generic utility casting.

development.note: The script is clear on the setup and payoff, but the mythology around SINONs, the erased-memory flash, and the exact rules of Francis's power are still more implied than fully dramatized.

comp_set.title: Shaun of the Dead
comp_set.why_it_comps: The ordinary-guy-under-pressure structure and comic escalation into violent genre action are the same basic engine, even though this script swaps zombies-for-bureaucratic-monsters.

comp_set.title: The Boys
comp_set.why_it_comps: The irreverent, profane superpowered workplace energy and the sense of a corrupt system managing dangerous anomalies feel adjacent in tone and audience.

comp_set.title: Deadpool
comp_set.why_it_comps: The script shares the self-aware, joke-forward action rhythm and the willingness to let absurdity coexist with real violence.

comp_set.title: R.I.P.D.
comp_set.why_it_comps: A supernatural enforcement unit with oddball teammates and a reluctant recruit gives it a similar commercial lane, even if this script is more stylized and less broad.

audience_target.primary_audience: Genre audiences who want a funny, violent, high-concept team movie with a reluctant underdog lead and a weirdly specific world.
audience_target.demographics: 18-44 skew, male-leaning but with strong crossover for viewers who like ensemble action-comedy and elevated genre worldbuilding.

budget_tier.note: Contemporary office interiors keep the base manageable, but the creature work, night exterior action, teleportation/VFX, and ensemble stunt coverage push it into mid-budget genre territory.

types_of_buyers: streamer originals execs building a genre-comedy slate
mid-budget genre producers looking for a breakout franchise seed
financiers seeking a contained but stylized effects vehicle
lane_fit.detail: This sits naturally in the lane of smart, irreverent genre pieces that can sell on concept, ensemble chemistry, and a distinctive world rather than on tentpole scale. The script’s office-bureaucracy angle gives it a hook that is easy to market without requiring a giant canvas.

ip_potential.detail: Standalone feature: the world is expandable, but no supporting character or specific spinoff vector is developed deeply enough on the page to justify franchise planning.

strengths.dimension_or_area: The office-world hook is instantly ownable.
strengths.what_it_means: That gives the project a clean marketing angle: supernatural action filtered through bureaucratic absurdity, which is easier to pitch than a generic monster-hunting premise. Buyers looking for a fresh genre wrapper can see the trailer in their heads immediately.
strengths.evidence: The death-toll board, the logistics division, and Francis doing spreadsheet work while the team prepares to kill a British monster establish the premise in a few pages.

strengths.dimension_or_area: Francis is a strong reluctant-lead engine.
strengths.what_it_means: A lead who is visibly terrified, funny, and secretly dangerous is exactly the kind of role that can launch or reframe a young actor. Casting teams and managers will respond to the built-in arc from pencil pusher to accidental weapon.
strengths.evidence: His panic at being recruited, his repeated insistence that he does nothing, and the final beam attack all reinforce the contradiction.

strengths.dimension_or_area: The ensemble already plays like a team.
strengths.what_it_means: That creates repeatable scene energy and gives the project more than one casting lane, which is valuable for both package-building and audience retention. The script can sell on chemistry, not just premise.
strengths.evidence: Francis/Ploy banter, Hal’s bravado, Clara’s chaos, and Toast’s deadpan all land as distinct comic registers.

strengths.dimension_or_area: The tone is specific without feeling random.
strengths.what_it_means: A buyer can understand the lane quickly: profane, stylized, and action-forward, but still character-based. That kind of tonal control is what makes a genre script feel packageable instead of merely quirky.
strengths.evidence: Comic-sans death toll board, retro-futuristic weapons, and the British zombie’s absurd dialogue all sit in the same register.

strengths.dimension_or_area: The climax pays off the premise cleanly.
strengths.what_it_means: The script gives the audience a visible transformation moment and a satisfying use of the lead’s hidden ability, which is crucial for word-of-mouth genre value. It suggests a trailer-friendly final act with a clear hero beat.
strengths.evidence: Francis eating the hot dog, triggering the memory, and erasing the zombie with a multicolor beam is a clean payoff sequence.

whats_special.headline: This is a packageable mid-budget genre feature with a clean hook: office drudgery collides with monster-hunting mayhem, and the lead role is built to showcase a breakout comic actor. The contained workplace setup keeps the economics sane while the ensemble chemistry and stylized action give buyers a clear trailer and a clear lane.

items.area: The mythology is still mostly a tease.
items.detail: Francis's erased-memory flash, the SINON label, and the wrist percentage meter all imply a bigger system, but the page stops short of making the rules feel fully legible. That is not a deal-breaker for a genre buyer, but it does mean the script is still selling promise more than payoff on the world-building side.

items.area: The London fight is the budget pressure point.
items.detail: The rooftop chase, regeneration effects, limb-loss gags, teleportation flashes, and beam climax all stack into a sequence that will carry the cost above a simple contained indie. Producers will read this as a mid-budget genre swing, not a cheap contained comedy.

The script lives or dies on finding an actor who can play anxious, funny, and secretly powerful without flattening any of those notes. That narrows the casting conversation more than the page count suggests, because the role needs both comic timing and a late-action payoff.

items.area: The supporting team is vivid but lightly sketched.
items.detail: Hal, Clara, Toast, Ploy, and Jerry all pop in scene, but most of them are defined by a single strong comic trait or function. That makes the ensemble immediately entertaining, but it also means the script is not yet offering much depth beyond the lead for buyers thinking about long-term value.

issues.headline: The script’s biggest friction is that it is selling a larger mythology than it fully cashes on the page, so buyers will be asked to trust the world before they’ve fully seen its rules. The other conversation is economic: the final action sequence and creature effects push this into a real mid-budget genre lane, which is viable but not casual.
